## devonthink
CRITICAL — Database package safety: DEVONthink databases are stored as packages (.dtBase2) or sparse images (.dtSparse, .dtArchive). Never modify, rename, move, or delete files inside a database package directly via the filesystem. All record and content operations must go through this MCP server or, as a fallback, via AppleScript. Direct filesystem manipulation will corrupt the database and cause irreversible data loss.

Batch operations: Use the uuids array parameter instead of sequential single-record calls for tag, update, move, trash, duplicate, replicate, and export operations. Batch mode is faster, reduces round trips, and returns a summary with succeeded/failed counts.

Avoiding duplicates: Use lookup_records (by name, URL, path, filename, or comment) before create_record to check whether a record already exists.

Content editing: Prefer update_record_content with mode append or insert over replace for large documents. Replace mode requires sending the entire new content and risks accidental data loss if the content is incomplete.

Group hierarchies: Use create_group_path to create nested group structures in a single call (like mkdir -p) rather than sequential create_record calls.

AI-powered tools: classify_record and find_similar_records use DEVONthink's built-in AI algorithms and proprietary training data — they provide organizational suggestions that complement, not duplicate, your own capabilities.

Record enrichment: resolve_doi_metadata and resolve_book_metadata can enrich existing records with bibliographic metadata by passing the record's uuid — there is no need to create a new record.

AI exclusion: Records marked as excluded from AI access (excludeFromChat) are protected in two ways. (1) Input protection: any tool that receives such a record's UUID as an argument refuses to operate on it and returns an error. 1	# Spending Report Design
2	
3	**Date:** 2026-07-09
4	**Status:** v1 built (see [Implementation status](#implementation-status))
5	
6	## Overview
7	
8	A top-level **Spending** report that rolls up Expenses by **Importance →
9	Grouping → Category** across the months of a year. It replaces the Excel pivot
10	table the family currently maintains by hand. ("Spending Report" is the working
11	term; pin the final ubiquitous-language name in `domain-model.md` when built.)
12	
13	Built so far: the **table view** (v1) and the **chart view** (an accordion
14	magnitude bar chart) — see [Implementation status](#implementation-status) and
15	[Spending Chart](#spending-chart-graphical-presentation--built). Still deferred:
16	selectable periods, year-over-year comparison, historical-year upload, hierarchy
17	editing, and export (see [Deferred](#deferred-later-slices)).
18	
19	## Data model (new)
20	
21	The category hierarchy today is flat: `categories (family_id, name, color)`.
22	There is no Grouping or Importance layer. v1 adds two tiers as real,
23	family-scoped tables so they are first-class and become editable later.
24	
25	- `importance_areas (id, family_id, name, sort_order)` — e.g. Essential
26	  (sort_order 1), Priorities (2), Other (3). The numeric prefix in the sample
27	  (`1. Essential`) becomes `sort_order`, not part of the name.
28	- `category_groups (id, family_id, name, importance_area_id)` — **Importance
29	  attaches to the Grouping**, not to individual categories. Matches the sample
30	  (all of Transportation is Essential) and makes the roll-up a clean two-hop
31	  join. If a future need arises for two categories in one group to have
32	  different importances, revisit — no counterexample in the current sample.
33	- `categories` gains `group_id → category_groups`. A Category belongs to a
34	  Group; the Group carries the Importance.
35	
36	**Seeding.** Derive default Importance areas and Groupings from
37	`docs/SampleHierachy.txt` (cleaned). Map the existing default categories into
38	Groups by name. Near-duplicate categories in the sample (`Car - Insurance` vs
39	`Car insurance`, `Gas` vs `Car - Gas`, `Parking` vs `Car - Parking`) are **not
40	auto-merged** — recognizable names are mapped, the rest fall to Uncategorized.
41	New families are seeded via the same path as `createDefaultCategories`, so any
42	future family gets a working report out of the box.
43	
44	## Report content
45	
46	- **Source:** receipts/Expenses (the app's source of truth for spending), **not**
47	  bank transactions. Bucketed by `transaction_date` (purchase date, not upload
48	  date).
49	- **Currency:** normalized to the family's display currency —
50	  `total_amount × (exchange_rate_to_cad ?? 1)`. CAD for now; the assumption is
51	  isolated so multi-currency drops in later.
52	- **Columns:** January → the last month that has any expense (left edge stays at
53	  January for a stable calendar grid). Interior/empty cells render blank, not
54	  `$0.00`. Final column is labelled **"Year to Date."**
55	- **Rows:** four row types — category detail, **Grouping subtotal**,
56	  **Importance subtotal**, and a final **Grand Total**. Importance ordered by
57	  `sort_order` (Essential → Priorities → Other); Groupings alphabetical within an
58	  Importance; Categories alphabetical within a Grouping. **Zero-activity rows are
59	  suppressed** (a category/group with no spend in the visible window is hidden).
60	- **Uncategorized:** rendered as its own section at the bottom, outside the real
61	  Importance/Grouping subtotals. It **is included in the Grand Total** (and any
62	  month-column totals), so the bottom-right number ties out to the family's
63	  actual total spend. The gap between the three Importance subtotals and the
64	  Grand Total is the deliberate nudge to go categorize.
65	- **Null amounts:** counted as `$0`. No new flag — the receipts and expenses
66	  pages already badge these (`⚠ Amount not read`). At most a small "N receipts
67	  missing an amount" footnote deep-linking to that existing filtered view.
68	
69	## Architecture
70	
71	- **Client-side pure aggregation.** A tested pure function
72	  `buildSpendingReport(expenses, hierarchy, year) → grid`, in the style of the
73	  CSV parsers and date utilities. The small hierarchy tables and the year's
74	  expenses are fetched separately and joined in TypeScript — the existing
75	  expense query is not widened. A family's yearly receipt count is small, so the
76	  data transfer is negligible and the logic stays unit-testable. If volume ever
77	  demands it, swap in a Postgres RPC behind the same function boundary — this
78	  avoids the RLS-fragility minefield the codebase repeatedly warns about.
79	- **Placement:** a new top-level **`/spending`** tab, following the existing
80	  `resolve()` / `filterQuery` nav pattern. May be promoted to the home page
81	  later once proven (currently `/` is "Family Receipts") — a separate change.
82	- **No editing UI in v1.** The hierarchy is hand-maintained (direct SQL) while
83	  the family is a single maintainer. The Uncategorized bucket is the feedback
84	  loop for anything unmapped.
85	
86	## Implementation status
87	
88	v1 is built and running against live data (v0.50). What landed:
89	
90	- **Migration** `supabase/migrations/20260709_spending_hierarchy.sql` — creates
91	  `importance_areas` and `category_groups`, adds `categories.group_id`
92	  (`ON DELETE SET NULL`), family-scoped RLS mirroring `categories_family_access`,
93	  unique-per-family name indexes, and `updated_at` triggers. Ships
94	  `create_default_hierarchy(p_family_id)` (idempotent, `SECURITY DEFINER`): seeds
95	  3 Importance areas + 13 Groupings and maps categories → groups by name (a
96	  superset covering both the current default names and the older spreadsheet
97	  names). Backfills every existing family in a `DO` loop; the app calls it via
98	  RPC for new families.
99	- **Grouping → Importance seed choices.** Each Grouping is collapsed to a single
100	  Importance (the model attaches Importance to the Grouping): **Essential** =
101	  Everyday, Health, Home, Transportation, Income Taxes; **Priorities** = Banking
102	  & Investing, Debt, Fitness, Kids, Rental; **Other** = Discretionary, Gifts,
103	  Travel. Where the source spreadsheet split a Grouping across importances (e.g.
104	  Home's Garden/Household goods were "Other"), it now rolls up under the
105	  Grouping's single Importance. Change with a one-row `UPDATE` on
106	  `category_groups.importance_area_id`.
107	- **Aggregation** `src/lib/utils/spendingReport.ts` — the pure
108	  `buildSpendingReport(expenses, categories, groups, importanceAreas, year)`.
109	  21 unit tests in `spendingReport.spec.ts` (month columns, roll-up/subtotals,
110	  ordering, Uncategorized, refund netting, FX, null amounts, blank-vs-zero cells).
111	  Per-cell `{ amount, count }` drives blank (count 0) vs `0.00` (net-zero but had
112	  activity).
113	- **Types** `src/lib/types/Hierarchy.ts` (`ImportanceArea`, `CategoryGroup`);
114	  `Category` gains `group_id`.
115	- **Service** `CategoryService` gains `getFamilyImportanceAreas`,
116	  `getFamilyGroups`, and `createDefaultHierarchy` (RPC wrapper).
117	- **Page + nav** `src/routes/spending/+page.svelte` + a **Spending** top-level
118	  tab. Self-seeds the hierarchy on first open (mirrors default-categories
119	  lazy-init), then loads hierarchy + the year's expenses and paints the grid.
120	  Year prev/next selector, missing-amount footnote, Importance bands, Grouping
121	  and Importance subtotals, Uncategorized section, Grand Total.
122	- **Rendering details.** Long category names truncate to one line
123	  (`max-w-64 truncate`) with the full name on hover via `title`. The layout gives
124	  `/spending` full window width (`max-w-full`); other pages keep `max-w-5xl`.
125	
126	**Verification:** `npm run check`, `eslint`, and Prettier clean on touched files;
127	full unit suite green (1278 passed / 8 skipped, incl. the 21 new). Production
128	build succeeds. Not yet exercised: a rendered end-to-end pass (no local
129	auth/seed harness) — validated live by the maintainer instead.
130	
131	**Known open item surfaced by live data:** the seed maps by name, so any custom
132	or renamed category lands in Uncategorized until its `group_id` is set by hand.
133	
134	## Spending Chart (graphical presentation) — built
135	
136	A `Table | Chart` toggle on `/spending` (shared year selector + loaded data)
137	adds a **magnitude bar chart** view (v0.60).
138	
139	> **Design note — why not stacked-by-month.** The first cut stacked 12 month
140	> segments per bar with a sequential ramp. In real data it failed twice: the 12
141	> subtle shades read as noise ("the gradient is a mess"), and one dominant
142	> Grouping (a family's ~$33k Home, driven by a one-off $20k renovation) crushed
143	> every other bar's height so small bars were unreadable. Both flaws trace to the
144	> month stack. v0.60 drops it: **solid magnitude bars + value labels**, with the
145	> month/time story deferred to the separate trend chart.
146	
147	- **Form:** one **solid bar per Grouping** = its year-to-date total, **coloured by
148	  Area of Importance** (a validated 3-colour categorical palette: Essential
149	  `#4f46e5`, Priorities `#0d9488`, Other `#d97706`; Uncategorized neutral gray).
150	  Bars ordered by Importance `sort_order` then Grouping name; **Uncategorized**
151	  trails; zero-activity groups suppressed.
152	- **Value label** above every bar (formatted currency), so a tiny bar next to a
153	  dominant one is still readable — the fix for the outlier problem without a
154	  scale hack. Positioned from the bound LayerChart `context` (band x-scale +
155	  linear y-scale).
156	- **Two bracket rows beneath the axis** carry the hierarchy, both positioned from
157	  the bound `context` band x-scale (aligned on resize):
158	  - **Row 1 — Grouping ± toggles.** One keyboard-focusable `<button>` bracket per
159	    Grouping, spanning its bar(s), showing `+ Name` / `− Name`. This is the
160	    expand/collapse control (see interaction) and the Grouping label.
161	  - **Row 2 — Area of Importance**, labelled **once per contiguous run** of
162	    same-Importance bars, in that Importance's colour. Uncategorized has no
163	    Importance bracket (its Grouping bracket names it).
164	- **Interaction: expand in place (accordion), not drill-and-replace.** Clicking a
165	  Grouping's bar **or** its ± bracket expands it into its **Category** bars _in
166	  place_ while its siblings stay visible; **any number of Groupings can be open at
167	  once** (`expandedGroups` is a reactive `SvelteSet`). Expanded Categories keep the
168	  parent Grouping's Importance colour and sit inside the same Importance bracket.
169	  Bars are keyed by a unique id, not name, so same-named Categories across
170	  Groupings don't collide on the band scale.
171	- **Click + hover come from a custom per-bar overlay, not LayerChart.** LayerChart's
172	  own tooltip layer both swallows bar clicks and can't carry a month breakdown, so
173	  `tooltipContext` is disabled and a transparent full-height column is drawn over
174	  each bar (from the band scale). It handles the click (toggle its Grouping) and the
175	  hover, which shows a **tooltip with the bar's name, its per-month totals, and the
176	  grand total** — the monthly detail dropped from the bars themselves. The overlay
177	  columns are `aria-hidden`/non-focusable mouse affordances; the ± brackets remain
178	  the keyboard-accessible controls.
179	- **Long labels don't collide.** When a Grouping expands into many Category bars,
180	  each axis label is truncated to one bar width with an ellipsis (`Meals and Drinks
181	Out` → `Meals…`); the full name is in the hover tooltip. Collapsed Grouping names
182	  live in their ± bracket (truncated there too). The one-line usage hint sits below
183	  the chart.
184	- **Data:** no new aggregation — the pure
185	  `buildSpendingChart(report, expandedGroups)` reshapes the existing
186	  `SpendingReport` into a flat `{ months, bars }` where expanded Groupings
187	  contribute their Category bars in place (unit-tested in `spendingChart.spec.ts`).
188	  The per-bar `monthly` map is retained for the future trend chart / hover detail;
189	  the current view uses only `total`.
190	- **Library:** **LayerChart 2.0.1** (`<BarChart>` with `y="total"` and a `c`
191	  ordinal colour scale by Importance; `bandPadding`, rounded bars). Peer
192	  `svelte@^5`. Its built-in tooltip/click layer (`tooltipContext`) is **disabled**
193	  in favour of the custom overlay above. Colours validated with the dataviz palette
194	  script (CVD ΔE 57.8, contrast ≥ 3:1); identity carried by position + brackets,
195	  not colour alone.
196	- **Verification:** `SpendingChart.svelte.spec.ts` (8 tests) renders it in Chromium
197	  and asserts: a bar per Grouping lays out, the once-only Importance brackets, the
198	  per-bar value labels, expand-in-place (siblings stay), several open at once,
199	  collapse back, **the bar itself (not just the bracket) expands**, and **the hover
200	  tooltip shows name + month totals + grand total**. `spendingChart.spec.ts`
201	  (6 tests) covers the pure accordion model; `spendingReport.spec.ts` (21) the
202	  aggregation.
203	
204	**Chart known limitation:**
205	
206	- **Prior-period overlay** (a line above/below the bar) is **not built** — it
207	  depends on historical-year data, which isn't loaded yet. Deferred with the
208	  upload/YoY thread below. Month-by-month detail currently lives in the Table
209	  view; a dedicated trend chart is the natural home for it.
210	
211	## Planned — drill from a table cell into the Expenses view
212	
213	Make the table's numbers a jumping-off point: clicking a cell navigates to the
214	**Expenses** view, filtered to exactly the Expenses that produced that number.
215	
216	- **Category detail cell** (a category × month cell) → Expenses filtered to that
217	  **category** and that **month** (the month's start/end dates).
218	- **Category "Year to Date" cell** → that category across the whole selected year.
219	- **Subtotal cells** roll the filter up to match what they sum:
220	  - **Grouping subtotal** → all categories in that Grouping (that month, or YTD).
221	  - **Importance subtotal** → all categories in that Importance (that month, or YTD).
222	  - **Grand Total** → the whole year (optionally all categories).
223	  - **Uncategorized** cells → uncategorized Expenses for that month / the year.
224	- **Feasibility:** the Expenses page already filters by date range (`startDate` /
225	  `endDate`) and by one or more `categoryId`s, both URL-driven — so a cell links to
226	  `/expenses?...` with the month's dates plus the category id(s) the cell rolls up
227	  (a Grouping/Importance cell expands to its member category ids). Empty (blank)
228	  cells are not links. Consider the same affordance on chart bars later.
229	
230	## Deferred (later slices)
231	
232	- Prior-period overlay line + year-over-year comparison (needs historical data).
233	- Historical-year expense upload (unblocks the two above).
234	- Arbitrary period / quarter selection (beyond a single calendar year).
235	- The multi-chart-type menu and any second chart type (trend, magnitude).
236	- Hierarchy editing UI — both assigning categories to groups and restructuring
237	  the tiers (create/rename/reorder Groupings and Importance areas).
238	- Export (CSV / PDF).
239	- Promoting the report to the home page.
240	
241	## Known limitations (document when building)
242	
243	- **Refunds.** Refunds are represented as **negative `total_amount`** on a
244	  receipt (confirmed via `formatCurrency.spec.ts` and the export services). The
245	  report **keeps the sign**, so refunds net against spend — which is the correct
246	  behaviour for a spending total. (Note the CSV/PDF _exporters_ deliberately
247	  `abs()` refunds; the report does not.) One visible consequence: a Category or
248	  Grouping whose refunds exceed its spend in the window shows a **negative**
249	  total — informative, not a bug. No special handling needed in v1; documented
250	  here so the divergence from the exporters is intentional and searchable.
251	- **"Year to Date" label** reads oddly for a _completed past_ year (it is the
252	  full-year total). Relabel per-context when the multi-year slice lands. Not a
253	  v1 problem since v1 is current-year only.

magnitude bar chart) — see [Implementation status](#implementation-status) and
[Spending Chart](#spending-chart-graphical-presentation--built). Still deferred:
selectable periods, year-over-year comparison, historical-year upload, hierarchy
editing, and export (see [Deferred](#deferred-later-slices)).

## Data model (new)

The category hierarchy today is flat: `categories (family_id, name, color)`.
There is no Grouping or Importance layer. v1 adds two tiers as real,
family-scoped tables so they are first-class and become editable later.

- `importance_areas (id, family_id, name, sort_order)` — e.g. Essential
  (sort_order 1), Priorities (2), Other (3). The numeric prefix in the sample
  (`1. Essential`) becomes `sort_order`, not part of the name.
- `category_groups (id, family_id, name, importance_area_id)` — **Importance
  attaches to the Grouping**, not to individual categories. Matches the sample
  (all of Transportation is Essential) and makes the roll-up a clean two-hop
  join. If a future need arises for two categories in one group to have
  different importances, revisit — no counterexample in the current sample.
- `categories` gains `group_id → category_groups`. A Category belongs to a
  Group; the Group carries the Importance.

**Seeding.** Derive default Importance areas and Groupings from
`docs/SampleHierachy.txt` (cleaned). Map the existing default categories into
Groups by name. Near-duplicate categories in the sample (`Car - Insurance` vs
`Car insurance`, `Gas` vs `Car - Gas`, `Parking` vs `Car - Parking`) are **not
auto-merged** — recognizable names are mapped, the rest fall to Uncategorized.
New families are seeded via the same path as `createDefaultCategories`, so any
future family gets a working report out of the box.

## Report content

- **Source:** receipts/Expenses (the app's source of truth for spending), **not**
  bank transactions. Bucketed by `transaction_date` (purchase date, not upload
  date).
- **Currency:** normalized to the family's display currency —
  `total_amount × (exchange_rate_to_cad ?? 1)`. CAD for now; the assumption is
  isolated so multi-currency drops in later.
- **Columns:** January → the last month that has any expense (left edge stays at
  January for a stable calendar grid). Interior/empty cells render blank, not
  `$0.00`. Final column is labelled **"Year to Date."**
- **Rows:** four row types — category detail, **Grouping subtotal**,
  **Importance subtotal**, and a final **Grand Total**. Importance ordered by
  `sort_order` (Essential → Priorities → Other); Groupings alphabetical within an
  Importance; Categories alphabetical within a Grouping. **Zero-activity rows are
  suppressed** (a category/group with no spend in the visible window is hidden).
- **Uncategorized:** rendered as its own section at the bottom, outside the real
  Importance/Grouping subtotals. It **is included in the Grand Total** (and any
  month-column totals), so the bottom-right number ties out to the family's
  actual total spend. The gap between the three Importance subtotals and the
  Grand Total is the deliberate nudge to go categorize.
- **Null amounts:** counted as `$0`. No new flag — the receipts and expenses
  pages already badge these (`⚠ Amount not read`). At most a small "N receipts
  missing an amount" footnote deep-linking to that existing filtered view.

## Architecture

- **Client-side pure aggregation.** A tested pure function
  `buildSpendingReport(expenses, hierarchy, year) → grid`, in the style of the
  CSV parsers and date utilities. The small hierarchy tables and the year's
  expenses are fetched separately and joined in TypeScript — the existing
  expense query is not widened. A family's yearly receipt count is small, so the
  data transfer is negligible and the logic stays unit-testable. If volume ever
  demands it, swap in a Postgres RPC behind the same function boundary — this
  avoids the RLS-fragility minefield the codebase repeatedly warns about.
- **Placement:** a new top-level **`/spending`** tab, following the existing
  `resolve()` / `filterQuery` nav pattern. May be promoted to the home page
  later once proven (currently `/` is "Family Receipts") — a separate change.
- **No editing UI in v1.** The hierarchy is hand-maintained (direct SQL) while
  the family is a single maintainer. The Uncategorized bucket is the feedback
  loop for anything unmapped.

## Implementation status

v1 is built and running against live data (v0.50). What landed:

- **Migration** `supabase/migrations/20260709_spending_hierarchy.sql` — creates
  `importance_areas` and `category_groups`, adds `categories.group_id`
  (`ON DELETE SET NULL`), family-scoped RLS mirroring `categories_family_access`,
  unique-per-family name indexes, and `updated_at` triggers. Ships
  `create_default_hierarchy(p_family_id)` (idempotent, `SECURITY DEFINER`): seeds
  3 Importance areas + 13 Groupings and maps categories → groups by name (a
  superset covering both the current default names and the older spreadsheet
  names). Backfills every existing family in a `DO` loop; the app calls it via
  RPC for new families.
- **Grouping → Importance seed choices.** Each Grouping is collapsed to a single
  Importance (the model attaches Importance to the Grouping): **Essential** =
  Everyday, Health, Home, Transportation, Income Taxes; **Priorities** = Banking
  & Investing, Debt, Fitness, Kids, Rental; **Other** = Discretionary, Gifts,
  Travel. Where the source spreadsheet split a Grouping across importances (e.g.
  Home's Garden/Household goods were "Other"), it now rolls up under the
  Grouping's single Importance. Change with a one-row `UPDATE` on
  `category_groups.importance_area_id`.
- **Aggregation** `src/lib/utils/spendingReport.ts` — the pure
  `buildSpendingReport(expenses, categories, groups, importanceAreas, year)`.
  21 unit tests in `spendingReport.spec.ts` (month columns, roll-up/subtotals,
  ordering, Uncategorized, refund netting, FX, null amounts, blank-vs-zero cells).
  Per-cell `{ amount, count }` drives blank (count 0) vs `0.00` (net-zero but had
  activity).
- **Types** `src/lib/types/Hierarchy.ts` (`ImportanceArea`, `CategoryGroup`);
  `Category` gains `group_id`.
- **Service** `CategoryService` gains `getFamilyImportanceAreas`,
  `getFamilyGroups`, and `createDefaultHierarchy` (RPC wrapper).
- **Page + nav** `src/routes/spending/+page.svelte` + a **Spending** top-level
  tab. Self-seeds the hierarchy on first open (mirrors default-categories
  lazy-init), then loads hierarchy + the year's expenses and paints the grid.
  Year prev/next selector, missing-amount footnote, Importance bands, Grouping
  and Importance subtotals, Uncategorized section, Grand Total.
- **Rendering details.** Long category names truncate to one line
  (`max-w-64 truncate`) with the full name on hover via `title`. The layout gives
  `/spending` full window width (`max-w-full`); other pages keep `max-w-5xl`.

**Verification:** `npm run check`, `eslint`, and Prettier clean on touched files;
full unit suite green (1278 passed / 8 skipped, incl. the 21 new). Production
build succeeds. Not yet exercised: a rendered end-to-end pass (no local
auth/seed harness) — validated live by the maintainer instead.

**Known open item surfaced by live data:** the seed maps by name, so any custom
or renamed category lands in Uncategorized until its `group_id` is set by hand.

## Spending Chart (graphical presentation) — built

A `Table | Chart` toggle on `/spending` (shared year selector + loaded data)
adds a **magnitude bar chart** view (v0.60).

> **Design note — why not stacked-by-month.** The first cut stacked 12 month
> segments per bar with a sequential ramp. In real data it failed twice: the 12
> subtle shades read as noise ("the gradient is a mess"), and one dominant
> Grouping (a family's ~$33k Home, driven by a one-off $20k renovation) crushed
> every other bar's height so small bars were unreadable. Both flaws trace to the
> month stack. v0.60 drops it: **solid magnitude bars + value labels**, with the
> month/time story deferred to the separate trend chart.

- **Form:** one **solid bar per Grouping** = its year-to-date total, **coloured by
  Area of Importance** (a validated 3-colour categorical palette: Essential
  `#4f46e5`, Priorities `#0d9488`, Other `#d97706`; Uncategorized neutral gray).
  Bars ordered by Importance `sort_order` then Grouping name; **Uncategorized**
  trails; zero-activity groups suppressed.
- **Value label** above every bar (formatted currency), so a tiny bar next to a
  dominant one is still readable — the fix for the outlier problem without a
  scale hack. Positioned from the bound LayerChart `context` (band x-scale +
  linear y-scale).
- **Two bracket rows beneath the axis** carry the hierarchy, both positioned from
  the bound `context` band x-scale (aligned on resize):
  - **Row 1 — Grouping ± toggles.** One keyboard-focusable `<button>` bracket per
    Grouping, spanning its bar(s), showing `+ Name` / `− Name`. This is the
    expand/collapse control (see interaction) and the Grouping label.
  - **Row 2 — Area of Importance**, labelled **once per contiguous run** of
    same-Importance bars, in that Importance's colour. Uncategorized has no
    Importance bracket (its Grouping bracket names it).
- **Interaction: expand in place (accordion), not drill-and-replace.** Clicking a
  Grouping's bar **or** its ± bracket expands it into its **Category** bars _in
  place_ while its siblings stay visible; **any number of Groupings can be open at
  once** (`expandedGroups` is a reactive `SvelteSet`). Expanded Categories keep the
  parent Grouping's Importance colour and sit inside the same Importance bracket.
  Bars are keyed by a unique id, not name, so same-named Categories across
  Groupings don't collide on the band scale.
- **Click + hover come from a custom per-bar overlay, not LayerChart.** LayerChart's
  own tooltip layer both swallows bar clicks and can't carry a month breakdown, so
  `tooltipContext` is disabled and a transparent full-height column is drawn over
  each bar (from the band scale). It handles the click (toggle its Grouping) and the
  hover, which shows a **tooltip with the bar's name, its per-month totals, and the
  grand total** — the monthly detail dropped from the bars themselves. The overlay
  columns are `aria-hidden`/non-focusable mouse affordances; the ± brackets remain
  the keyboard-accessible controls.
- **Long labels don't collide.** When a Grouping expands into many Category bars,
  each axis label is truncated to one bar width with an ellipsis (`Meals and Drinks
Out` → `Meals…`); the full name is in the hover tooltip. Collapsed Grouping names
  live in their ± bracket (truncated there too). The one-line usage hint sits below
  the chart.
- **Data:** no new aggregation — the pure
  `buildSpendingChart(report, expandedGroups)` reshapes the existing
  `SpendingReport` into a flat `{ months, bars }` where expanded Groupings
  contribute their Category bars in place (unit-tested in `spendingChart.spec.ts`).
  The per-bar `monthly` map is retained for the future trend chart / hover detail;
  the current view uses only `total`.
- **Library:** **LayerChart 2.0.1** (`<BarChart>` with `y="total"` and a `c`
  ordinal colour scale by Importance; `bandPadding`, rounded bars). Peer
  `svelte@^5`. Its built-in tooltip/click layer (`tooltipContext`) is **disabled**
  in favour of the custom overlay above. Colours validated with the dataviz palette
  script (CVD ΔE 57.8, contrast ≥ 3:1); identity carried by position + brackets,
  not colour alone.
- **Verification:** `SpendingChart.svelte.spec.ts` (8 tests) renders it in Chromium
  and asserts: a bar per Grouping lays out, the once-only Importance brackets, the
  per-bar value labels, expand-in-place (siblings stay), several open at once,
  collapse back, **the bar itself (not just the bracket) expands**, and **the hover
  tooltip shows name + month totals + grand total**. `spendingChart.spec.ts`
  (6 tests) covers the pure accordion model; `spendingReport.spec.ts` (21) the
  aggregation.

**Chart known limitation:**

- **Prior-period overlay** (a line above/below the bar) is **not built** — it
  depends on historical-year data, which isn't loaded yet. Deferred with the
  upload/YoY thread below. Month-by-month detail currently lives in the Table
  view; a dedicated trend chart is the natural home for it.

## Planned — drill from a table cell into the Expenses view

Make the table's numbers a jumping-off point: clicking a cell navigates to the
**Expenses** view, filtered to exactly the Expenses that produced that number.

- **Category detail cell** (a category × month cell) → Expenses filtered to that
  **category** and that **month** (the month's start/end dates).
- **Category "Year to Date" cell** → that category across the whole selected year.
- **Subtotal cells** roll the filter up to match what they sum:
  - **Grouping subtotal** → all categories in that Grouping (that month, or YTD).
  - **Importance subtotal** → all categories in that Importance (that month, or YTD).
  - **Grand Total** → the whole year (optionally all categories).
  - **Uncategorized** cells → uncategorized Expenses for that month / the year.
- **Feasibility:** the Expenses page already filters by date range (`startDate` /
  `endDate`) and by one or more `categoryId`s, both URL-driven — so a cell links to
  `/expenses?...` with the month's dates plus the category id(s) the cell rolls up
  (a Grouping/Importance cell expands to its member category ids). Empty (blank)
  cells are not links. Consider the same affordance on chart bars later.

## Deferred (later slices)

- Prior-period overlay line + year-over-year comparison (needs historical data).
- Historical-year expense upload (unblocks the two above).
- Arbitrary period / quarter selection (beyond a single calendar year).
- The multi-chart-type menu and any second chart type (trend, magnitude).
- Hierarchy editing UI — both assigning categories to groups and restructuring
  the tiers (create/rename/reorder Groupings and Importance areas).
- Export (CSV / PDF).
- Promoting the report to the home page.

## Known limitations (document when building)

- **Refunds.** Refunds are represented as **negative `total_amount`** on a
  receipt (confirmed via `formatCurrency.spec.ts` and the export services). The
  report **keeps the sign**, so refunds net against spend — which is the correct
  behaviour for a spending total. (Note the CSV/PDF _exporters_ deliberately
  `abs()` refunds; the report does not.) One visible consequence: a Category or
  Grouping whose refunds exceed its spend in the window shows a **negative**
  total — informative, not a bug. No special handling needed in v1; documented
  here so the divergence from the exporters is intentional and searchable.
- **"Year to Date" label** reads oddly for a _completed past_ year (it is the
  full-year total). Relabel per-context when the multi-year slice lands. Not a
  v1 problem since v1 is current-year only.

Based on the design doc, the next best thing to implement is the **"drill from a table cell into the Expenses view"** feature (doc lines 211–228).

## Why this one

It's the only item the doc puts in a dedicated **"Planned"** section — everything else sits under **"Deferred (later slices)"**, and most of those are blocked on data you don't have yet (prior-period overlay, YoY, and the trend chart all wait on **historical-year upload**). This drill-down is:

# Test-Driven Development

TDD is the red → green loop. This skill is the reference that makes that loop produce tests worth keeping: what a good test is, where tests go, the anti-patterns, and the rules of the loop. Every section applies on every cycle — consult them before and during the loop, not after.

When exploring the codebase, read `CONTEXT.md` (if it exists) so test names and interface vocabulary match the project's domain language, and respect ADRs in the area you're touching.

## What a good test is

Tests verify behavior through public interfaces, not implementation details. Code can change entirely; tests shouldn't. A good test reads like a specification — "user can checkout with valid cart" tells you exactly what capability exists — and survives refactors because it doesn't care about internal structure.

See [tests.md](tests.md) for examples and [mocking.md](mocking.md) for mocking guidelines.

## Seams — where tests go

A **seam** is the public boundary you test at: the interface where you observe behavior without reaching inside. Tests live at seams, never against internals.

**Test only at pre-agreed seams.** Before writing any test, write down the seams under test and confirm them with the user. No test is written at an unconfirmed seam. You can't test everything — agreeing the seams up front is how testing effort lands on the critical paths and complex logic instead of every edge case.

Ask: "What's the public interface, and which seams should we test?"

## Anti-patterns

- **Implementation-coupled** — mocks internal collaborators, tests private methods, or verifies through a side channel (querying the database instead of using the interface). The tell: the test breaks when you refactor but behavior hasn't changed.
- **Tautological** — the assertion recomputes the expected value the way the code does (`expect(add(a, b)).toBe(a + b)`, a snapshot derived by hand the same way, a constant asserted equal to itself), so it passes by construction and can never disagree with the code. Expected values must come from an independent source of truth — a known-good literal, a worked example, the spec.
- **Horizontal slicing** — writing all tests first, then all implementation. Bulk tests verify _imagined_ behavior: you test the _shape_ of things rather than user-facing behavior, the tests go insensitive to real changes, and you commit to test structure before understanding the implementation. Work in **vertical slices** instead — one test → one implementation → repeat, each test a **tracer bullet** that responds to what the last cycle taught you.

## Rules of the loop

- **Red before green.** Write the failing test first, then only enough code to pass it. Don't anticipate future tests or add speculative features.
- **One slice at a time.** One seam, one test, one minimal implementation per cycle.
- **Refactoring is not part of the loop.** It belongs to the review stage (see the `code-review` skill), not the red → green implementation cycle.

The table's numbers are a jumping-off point (v0.55): clicking a non-blank cell
navigates to the **Expenses** view, filtered to exactly the Expenses that

  - **Grouping subtotal** → every category id in that Grouping (that month/YTD).
  - **Importance subtotal** → every category id across the Importance's groups.
  - **Grand Total** → the date range alone (no category filter) so it ties out to
    all Expenses, **including Uncategorized**.
  - **Uncategorized** cells → the `filter=uncategorized` Expenses filter. A
    named-but-ungrouped category row instead drills to its own category id
    (precise); only the section subtotal and the "(No category)" row use the
    coarse `filter=uncategorized` (which by design covers only null-category
    Expenses, so a subtotal with ungrouped-category rows is a slight over-scope).

The function-definition grep missed it precisely _because_ it inlines the logic rather than defining a helper — so the "no others remain" claim was wrong. Replaced with a render test `ReceiptImageViewer.svelte.spec.ts` (8 tests) that drives the real zoom buttons/keyboard and asserts the visible zoom %, disabled boundaries, and close wiring (teeth-proven; ~91 tautologies → 8 real). Pointer gestures (wheel/pan/pinch) remain the separate manual-verify item. Heuristic lesson: audit for _inline_ reimplementation, not just `function`-defined helpers.
